citations.quote: Dijana Radulović
A Pre-Compliance Workflow for Mixed-Signal PCBs Integrating Near-Field Scanning, FDTD Simulation, and Layout Rule Checking

This paper describes an integrated pre-compliance workflow for mixed-signal PCB development that combines three techniques used sequentially across the design cycle. In the early layout phase, an automated rule-checking tool flags geometric violations associated with known emission risks. At the prototype stage, near-field scanning at 3 mm standoff generates spatial emission maps that identify dominant radiating structures. Finally, FDTD simulation using geometry extracted from the identified hotspots provides frequency-resolved quantification and supports what-if analysis of corrective measures. The workflow was applied to four prototype boards developed in collaboration with two regional electronics companies. Across all four boards, the integrated workflow identified the dominant emission source correctly in each case; corrective measures applied on the basis of simulation results reduced the peak radiated emission at the pre-compliance test receiver by between 5.2 dB and 11.7 dB before formal OATS measurement. Time-to-compliance for the four designs averaged 2.1 fewer test-and-rework cycles compared to a historical baseline of designs developed without structured pre-compliance analysis. The workflow documentation and rule-checker code are deposited in an open repository.

citations.quote: Dijana Radulović
Automated PCB Layout Scoring for EMC Risk Using Feature Extraction and a Rule-Based Engine

Manual EMC design review is time-consuming and relies on reviewer expertise that varies across organisations. This paper describes a rule-based layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and a netlist, extracts geometric features related to emission risk, and outputs a numerical score and flagged violation list. Seventeen rules were derived from simulation studies and published guidelines, covering trace-to-plane spacing, clock trace routing distance from board edge, decoupling capacitor placement relative to device power pins, and via stub length. The tool was implemented in Python using open-source Gerber parsing libraries. Validation was performed by scoring 23 PCB designs of known emission performance; boards that failed CISPR 22 Class B measurements scored below the threshold in 19 out of 23 cases (83% sensitivity). False-positive rate was 22%. Run time for a 20-layer board with 4000 components averaged 38 seconds. The tool is intended as an early design gate rather than a replacement for simulation or pre-compliance measurement.

proposal.rationale: Nexara Embedded d.o.o. faces a specific challenge where three of their last five PCB designs failed radiated emissions at a third-party EMC lab on the first submission, typically between 150-450 MHz. This results in an average cost of 9000 euros per re-test visit and delays client projects by six to ten weeks. To address this, the company has an rd_capacity of allocating one senior hardware engineer and one firmware engineer part-time to a collaborative project, with access to their lab equipment and internal board archives under NDA. Dijana Radulović (R0637) offers relevant substantive work and expertise, as documented in SYN-PUB-07261, which describes an automated rule-based layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and netlists to extract geometric features related to emission risk and flags violations. The specific technical mechanism to transfer is the automated rule-based layout scoring and feature extraction engine that evaluates trace-to-plane spacing, clock trace routing distance from board edge, decoupling capacitor placement, and via stub lengths from Gerber files and netlists. Transferring this capability remains a hypothesis because the rules derived from academic simulation and general guidelines must be validated against Nexara's specific historical board archives, stack-ups, and component libraries operating in the 150-450 MHz range before it can reliably prevent first-submission failures.

facts.quote: Three of our last five PCB designs failed radiated emissions at a third-party EMC lab on the first submission, typically between 150–450 MHz, which costs us on average €9,000 per re-test visit and delays client projects by six to ten weeks; we need a systematic way to predict and fix emission hotspots during layout review rather than after the fact.
We can allocate one senior hardware engineer and one firmware engineer part-time to a collaborative project, with access to our lab equipment and internal board archives under NDA.
Automated PCB Layout Scoring for EMC Risk Using Feature Extraction and a Rule-Based Engine

Manual EMC design review is time-consuming and relies on reviewer expertise that varies across organisations. This paper describes a rule-based layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and a netlist, extracts geometric features related to emission risk, and outputs a numerical score and flagged violation list. Seventeen rules were derived from simulation studies and published guidelines, covering trace-to-plane spacing, clock trace routing distance from board edge, decoupling capacitor placement relative to device power pins, and via stub length. The tool was implemented in Python using open-source Gerber parsing libraries. Validation was performed by scoring 23 PCB designs of known emission performance; boards that failed CISPR 22 Class B measurements scored below the threshold in 19 out of 23 cases (83% sensitivity). False-positive rate was 22%. Run time for a 20-layer board with 4000 components averaged 38 seconds. The tool is intended as an early design gate rather than a replacement for simulation or pre-compliance measurement.

plan.question: Can an automated rule-based layout scoring tool trained on geometric feature extraction be calibrated to predict 150-450 MHz emission hotspots in Nexara's board designs? If the pilot succeeds, a conditional industrial PhD research question for after the pilot is: How can machine-learning-augmented geometric rule extraction adapt dynamically to complex multi-layer stack-ups to eliminate first-submission EMC failures?
plan.experiment: Ingest historical Gerber files, BOMs, and pre-compliance scan data from Nexara's five recent PCB designs into the Python-based rule-based scoring engine to evaluate correlation with known 150-450 MHz emission failures.
plan.metrics: Sensitivity of identifying known failing boards, false-positive rate, and execution time per design layout.
plan.companyAsk: Allocation of one senior hardware engineer and one firmware engineer part-time, plus access to lab equipment and internal board archives under NDA.
plan.researcherAsk: Access to the Python-based rule-based scoring tool framework and guidance on feature extraction rules.
plan.milestones: Week 2: Data packaging and NDA execution. Week 4: Initial baseline scoring run on historical board archives. Week 6: Rule calibration for 150-450 MHz frequency range. Week 8: Final evaluation report and handoff.
plan.risks: Proprietary stack-up variations not captured by standard rules; high false-positive rates masking real emission hotspots.
plan.meeting: Week 1 kickoff agenda: review NDA terms, outline board archive format, define data transfer protocols, and establish weekly sync schedules.
plan.terms: Negotiable bilateral terms covering background IP protection, data confidentiality under NDA, and results ownership for the joint pilot.

previousOutput.interpretation: Jelena Marković is the author of the cited publication on mixed-berry packaging which evaluates polymeric packaging films differing in OTR and CO2TR for MAP of berry trays, uses finite element modelling of gas permeation to confirm experimental headspace trends, and demonstrates reduced mold incidence, directly addressing the challenge of matching OTR to berry respiration and modeling headspace parameters.

citations.quote: Jelena Marković
Packaging material permeability screening for MAP of mixed-berry trays

Mixed-berry trays combining raspberry, blueberry, and blackberry are commercially attractive but present packaging engineering challenges because each species has a distinct optimal modified atmosphere range and a different respiration rate at equivalent temperatures. This study evaluated 12 commercially available polymeric packaging films differing in oxygen transmission rate (OTR) and carbon dioxide transmission rate (CO₂TR) for their suitability in MAP of mixed-berry trays stored at 2 °C. Headspace equilibrium gas compositions were measured at 24-hour intervals over eight days and compared against species-specific target ranges determined from prior single-species trials. Microbiological and firmness data were collected at four-day intervals. A film with OTR of 3,800 cm³/m²/day and CO₂TR of 18,000 cm³/m²/day delivered headspace conditions within acceptable ranges for all three species simultaneously and reduced mold incidence by 55% relative to a standard polyethylene control. Finite element modelling of gas permeation through the film was used to confirm experimental headspace trends and to predict equilibrium under alternative tray fill-weight scenarios. The results provide film specification guidance for packers handling mixed-berry formats and demonstrate that a single film solution can satisfy the conflicting atmosphere requirements of co-packaged fruit species.
